title: Market Sizing — TAM, SAM, SOM
summary: Three nested estimates of how big the opportunity is, and why the third is the only honest one.
what: **TAM** (total addressable market) is everyone who could conceivably buy. **SAM** (serviceable addressable market) is the part your product and reach could actually serve. **SOM** (serviceable obtainable market) is what you could realistically win in a defined period.
why: The numbers get used to justify investment, and a TAM figure with no SOM behind it justifies anything. The value of the exercise is the assumptions it forces you to write down, not the number it produces.
analogy: Everyone in the city who eats (TAM), everyone within delivery range who eats your cuisine (SAM), and everyone you can realistically serve next year given the kitchen (SOM).
technical:
Two methods, and you should do both:

**Top-down** — start from an industry figure and narrow by segment. Fast, and inherits whatever assumptions the analyst made.

**Bottom-up** — number of potential customers × what each would pay × realistic penetration. Slower, and every input is arguable, which is the point.

**When the two disagree by an order of magnitude, the bottom-up one is usually closer** and the gap is where the interesting question is.

**SOM is where the honesty lives.** TAM is a large number that impresses nobody who has seen many of them. SOM requires stating your reach, your conversion rate and your capacity, all of which can be checked.

**For AI products the sizing has a specific trap: the willingness-to-pay assumption.** Because model capability is broadly available, a competitor can offer a similar capability quickly, so a sizing built on "everyone who has this problem will pay us $X" ignores that the price is under downward pressure from the moment you launch. Size on what your *differentiated* layer is worth — the data, the workflow integration, the trust — not on what the capability is worth.

example.caption: Top-down and bottom-up, and what the gap revealed
example.code:
# PRODUCT  an AI policy assistant sold to support organisations

# ── TOP-DOWN ───────────────────────────────────────────────
top_down = {
    "global customer service software":  58_000_000_000,
    "× AI-assist segment share":          0.08,
    "× our geography (India + SEA)":      0.06,
    "× mid-market (our segment)":         0.35,
}
tam_td = 58e9 * 0.08 * 0.06 * 0.35
print(f"top-down SAM: ${tam_td/1e6:.0f}M")     # $97M

# ── BOTTOM-UP ──────────────────────────────────────────────
bottom_up = {
    "mid-market support orgs in region":  4_200,
    "× have >30 agents (our threshold)":     0.45,
    "× would consider a new vendor/yr":      0.15,
    "annual contract value":              18_000,
}
sam_bu = 4200 * 0.45 * 18_000
som    = 4200 * 0.45 * 0.15 * 18_000
print(f"bottom-up SAM: ${sam_bu/1e6:.0f}M")    # $34M
print(f"SOM (year 1, 8% win rate): ${som*0.08/1e6:.1f}M")  # $0.4M

# ⚠ THE GAP: $97M top-down vs $34M bottom-up.
#   Nearly 3x. The bottom-up number is built from a customer
#   count we can name and a contract value we have quoted.
#   The top-down number inherits four multipliers we invented.
#
#   The interesting question is not "which is right" — it is
#   WHY they differ. Here: the top-down figure counts support
#   orgs with fewer than 30 agents, for whom the product does
#   not pay for itself. That is a real segment boundary the
#   top-down method cannot see.

# ── ⚠ THE PRICE PRESSURE TEST ──────────────────────────────
def with_price_pressure(acv, years, annual_decline):
    return [round(acv * (1 - annual_decline) ** y) for y in range(years)]

print(with_price_pressure(18_000, 4, 0.18))
# [18000, 14760, 12103, 9924]
#
# ⚠ If our value proposition is "AI answers policy questions",
#   the capability is commoditising and ~18%/yr price erosion
#   is optimistic, not pessimistic.
#
#   If it is "answers grounded in YOUR six years of resolved
#   tickets, inside the console your agents already use, with
#   an evaluation harness you own" — that is not commoditising
#   at the same rate, because it is not the model.
#
#   The sizing exercise's real output was that sentence.

questions.a: Every input is arguable and checkable — customer counts, contract values, penetration. Top-down inherits multipliers you cannot inspect, and a gap between the two usually points at a real segment boundary.

questions.q: What is the AI-specific trap in market sizing?

questions.a: The assumptions it forces you to write down. A number without stated reach, conversion and capacity justifies anything.

title: Competitive Analysis
summary: Understanding who you are actually competing with — usually not who you think.
what: Competitive analysis maps who else solves the problem your customers have, how they solve it, and what that implies for your position.
why: Teams analyse the companies that look like them and ignore the alternatives customers actually use — a spreadsheet, a colleague, or doing nothing. Those are usually the real competition and the hardest to displace.
analogy: A restaurant studying other restaurants while its customers are cooking at home.
technical:
**Define competition by the job, not by the category.** If customers hire a spreadsheet and a colleague, those are the competitors and their advantages are real — free, familiar, trusted, already integrated into how people work.

**Non-consumption is the most common competitor and the most underestimated.** Doing nothing has zero switching cost and no procurement process.

What to actually compare: how each alternative performs the job, what it costs including effort, what switching costs it carries, and what it cannot do.

**Feature-by-feature comparison tables are usually a distraction.** They lead to matching competitors rather than choosing a position, and a product that matches everything is differentiated by nothing.

**For AI products, the analysis has a specific shape.** Most competitors are calling the same models, so comparing capability is comparing the same thing. The meaningful axes are: whose data is better, whose workflow integration is deeper, who has distribution, and who can improve fastest — which comes back to evaluation infrastructure.

**Watch adjacent incumbents.** The platform your customers already use adding a passable version of your feature is the most common way a specialised AI product loses, and it does not require them to be better — only present.

title: Competitive Advantage & Moats
summary: What stops a competitor copying you — and why model quality is not on the list.
what: A competitive advantage is something that lets you deliver more value or at lower cost than competitors. A moat is an advantage that persists, because copying it is expensive, slow or structurally impossible.
why: Everything else in strategy depends on this question. An advantage that a competitor can replicate in a quarter is a head start, not a position, and planning as though it were a position is how companies lose markets they created.
analogy: A head start in a race versus a shorter route. The first is consumed as you run; the second stays yours.
technical:
The durable sources:
- **Network effects** — the product improves as more people use it. The strongest and the rarest.
- **Switching costs** — leaving is expensive in data, workflow, training or integration.
- **Proprietary data** — data you have that competitors cannot obtain, that measurably improves the product.
- **Scale economics** — unit costs fall as you grow.
- **Distribution** — you are already where the customer is.
- **Brand and trust** — expensive and slow to build, particularly in regulated contexts.
- **Regulatory position** — licences, certifications, approvals.

**For AI products specifically, four things are frequently mistaken for moats and are not:**
- **Model quality.** Available to competitors on the same terms and improving for everyone simultaneously.
- **Prompt engineering.** Copyable in an afternoon by anyone who sees the output.
- **Being first.** Consumed rapidly in a fast-moving field.
- **A fine-tuned model** on generic data. The base improves faster than your fine-tune, and often overtakes it.

**What is genuinely defensible:** proprietary data with a feedback loop, deep workflow integration that creates switching costs, distribution, and **evaluation infrastructure** — because it determines the *rate* at which you improve, which compounds in a way a static advantage does not.

The test: **if a well-funded competitor with the same model access started tomorrow, what would take them longest?** That is your moat. If the answer is "nothing much", you do not have one, and that is worth knowing.

questions.q: What is the test for whether something is a moat?
questions.a: If a well-funded competitor with the same model access started tomorrow, what would take them longest? Anything they could replicate in a quarter is a head start, not a position.

questions.q: Why is model quality not a moat?
questions.a: It is available to competitors on identical terms and improves for everyone simultaneously. The same applies to prompt engineering, which is copyable in an afternoon from the visible output.

questions.q: Why is evaluation infrastructure the strongest AI advantage?
questions.a: It determines the rate at which you improve, and a rate compounds. A competitor without it does not just start behind — they improve more slowly, because they cannot tell which changes helped.

interview.s30: A moat is an advantage that persists because copying it is hard. For AI products, model quality, prompt engineering and being first are all head starts rather than moats — competitors have the same model access.
interview.s90: The exercise I run is a copy test: a well-funded competitor with the same API access starts tomorrow, how long does each element take them? On a support assistant the answers were sobering — prompt engineering one day, retrieval architecture two weeks, model choice one hour, UI three weeks. Everything visible was under six weeks. What could not be copied was our customers' six years of labelled resolved tickets, the console integration with its procurement cycle, and the per-tenant golden set with the support leads who judge it. And the one that actually matters is the last one, because it compounds — the evaluation loop determines how fast we improve, so a competitor starting today does not just start behind, they improve more slowly. The uncomfortable strategic consequence is to stop investing in the visible layers as differentiators, which is exactly where all the demo-able product work lives.

title: Network Effects
summary: When each additional user makes the product better for everyone already there.
what: A network effect exists when the value of a product increases as more people use it. It is the strongest form of competitive advantage because the advantage grows on its own.
why: It is the most claimed and least possessed property in product strategy. Distinguishing a real network effect from ordinary growth changes what you should invest in, and most products claiming one have scale economics instead.
analogy: A telephone network. One telephone is useless; the millionth makes every existing one more valuable. Contrast a bakery, which does not bake better bread because it has more customers.
technical:
The types:
- **Direct** — more users of the same type make it better. Messaging, marketplaces on a single side.
- **Indirect (two-sided)** — more of one type attracts more of the other. Buyers and sellers, riders and drivers.
- **Data network effects** — usage generates data that improves the product for everyone. The one most relevant to AI, and the one most often claimed without substance.

**The test for a data network effect** is whether the data from user N measurably improves the experience of users 1 through N−1, and whether that improvement is something a competitor cannot obtain otherwise. Most "our AI learns from usage" claims fail both parts: the data improves nothing measurable, or the same improvement is available from public data.

**Local network effects can be stronger than global ones.** A tool that is valuable because *your team* uses it does not need global scale, and it is harder to displace, because switching requires coordinating a group rather than one person.

**Negative network effects exist.** Congestion, noise, declining quality of matches as a marketplace grows indiscriminately.

**Beware the confusion with scale economics.** Cheaper unit costs at scale is a real advantage and a different one — it helps you, not your users, and it does not compound in the same way.

    operates within a tenant, not across all customers.
    That is still valuable, and it means growth in NEW tenants
    does not strengthen existing ones. Plan accordingly:
    the advantage is per-account depth, not aggregate scale.

CLAIM 2  "More usage means better embeddings."
  Test 1  Does it? → We use an off-the-shelf embedding model.
          Usage does not change it at all.
  ⚠ VERDICT: no network effect. This was a sentence in a deck
    that nobody had checked. What actually improves with usage
    is the retrieval METADATA — which questions map to which
    documents — and that is worth building deliberately rather
    than claiming accidentally.

CLAIM 3  "Our marketplace of prompt templates."
  Test 1  More template authors → more choice for buyers  ✓
          More buyers → more incentive to author            ✓
          → a genuine two-sided indirect network effect
  ⚠ BUT: negative network effect at scale. At 4,000 templates
    buyers cannot find good ones and quality perception falls.
  → the strategic work is CURATION, not growth. Adding
    templates past a point makes the product worse.

  One real-but-local, one imaginary, one real-with-a-ceiling.
  All three were described identically in the strategy deck
  as "network effects". The test is what separated them, and
  each implies completely different investment.

title: Switching Costs
summary: What it costs a customer to leave — and the difference between earned and imposed.
what: Switching costs are everything a customer must spend to move to an alternative: data migration, retraining, integration work, process change and risk.
why: They determine retention more reliably than satisfaction does. A customer who is unhappy but faces high switching costs stays; a delighted customer with none can leave on a whim.
analogy: Moving house versus changing a light bulb. The decision is dominated by the cost of moving, not by how much you like the new place.
technical:
The categories: **data** (history that does not transfer), **integration** (the work of rewiring systems), **process** (documented workflows built around the tool), **learning** (retraining people), **contractual** (terms and commitments), and **risk** (the possibility the new thing is worse).

**Earned versus imposed is the distinction that matters.** Earned switching costs come from accumulated value the customer benefits from — their history, their tuning, their integrations. Imposed ones come from deliberate obstruction — proprietary formats, no export, punitive terms. Both retain customers; only one survives contact with a competitor who offers migration assistance, and imposed costs generate the resentment that makes customers leave the moment they can.

title: Business Models
summary: How a product captures value — and why AI breaks some familiar models.
what: A business model describes how a product creates value, who pays, on what basis, and how the cost of delivery relates to what is charged.
why: AI features have a per-request marginal cost that conventional software does not. Models built on the assumption of near-zero delivery cost — unlimited seats, flat-rate plans — behave differently when every use costs money.
analogy: A gym membership when every visit costs the gym money. The all-you-can-use plan works when marginal cost is near zero and fails when it is not.
technical:
The common models: **subscription** (per seat or per organisation), **usage-based** (per request, per token, per outcome), **hybrid** (a base plus overage), **transaction fee**, **freemium**, and **enterprise licence**.

**The AI complication:** per-seat pricing with unlimited usage means your cost scales with engagement while your revenue does not. A power user can cost more than they pay, and the more successful the feature is, the worse this gets. Teams discover this when adoption succeeds.

The responses that work:
- **Hybrid** — a base fee with a generous included allowance and overage beyond it. Predictable for the customer, bounded for you.
- **Outcome pricing** — charge per resolved ticket or per completed task. Aligns with value and is harder to compare against competitors on unit price. Requires being able to measure the outcome reliably.
- **Tiered by capability** — cheaper model on lower tiers, better model higher. Aligns cost with price naturally.

**Freemium needs particular care.** A free tier with a real marginal cost is a subsidy that scales with adoption, so it needs hard usage caps rather than soft ones, and it needs a conversion path that is actually measured.

**Whatever the model, know your cost per unit of value delivered.** That number is what tells you whether a plan is profitable, and for AI features it moves with model prices, context length and adoption patterns.

    cost = queries_per_month * COST_PER_QUERY
    return {"queries": queries_per_month,
            "cost": round(cost, 2),
            "margin": round(PRICE_PER_SEAT - cost, 2),
            "margin_pct": round((PRICE_PER_SEAT - cost)/PRICE_PER_SEAT*100)}

for q in (100, 500, 1_200, 3_400, 8_000):
    print(seat_margin(q))

# {'queries': 100,   'cost': 1.16,  'margin': 38.84, 'margin_pct': 97}
# {'queries': 500,   'cost': 5.80,  'margin': 34.20, 'margin_pct': 86}
# {'queries': 1200,  'cost': 13.92, 'margin': 26.08, 'margin_pct': 65}
# {'queries': 3400,  'cost': 39.44, 'margin':  0.56, 'margin_pct':  1}  ⚠
# {'queries': 8000,  'cost': 92.80, 'margin': -52.80, 'margin_pct': -132} ⚠

# ⚠ BREAK-EVEN AT ~3,450 QUERIES/MONTH — about 165/working day.
#   That is a heavy user, and heavy users are exactly the ones
#   who love the product and renew.
#
#   THE MODEL PUNISHES SUCCESS. As adoption improves, blended
#   margin falls. Nothing in a conventional SaaS dashboard
#   makes this visible until it is a problem.

# ── ACTUAL DISTRIBUTION, month 9 ───────────────────────────
DIST = {100: 0.31, 500: 0.34, 1200: 0.22, 3400: 0.10, 8000: 0.03}
blended = sum(seat_margin(q)["margin"] * w for q, w in DIST.items())
print(round(blended, 2))    # 25.79 per seat — still healthy
#
# ⚠ But the distribution is SHIFTING RIGHT as adoption grows.
#   Modelled forward at current adoption growth: blended margin
#   crosses below 50% in about seven months.

# ── HYBRID: the fix ────────────────────────────────────────
def hybrid(queries, base=40, included=1500, overage=0.02):
    cost = queries * COST_PER_QUERY
    revenue = base + max(0, queries - included) * overage
    return round(revenue - cost, 2)

for q in (100, 500, 1_200, 3_400, 8_000):
    print(q, hybrid(q))

# 8000 37.2

title: Unit Economics
summary: Whether one customer is profitable, before asking whether the business is.
what: Unit economics is the revenue and cost associated with a single unit — usually one customer, sometimes one transaction — over its lifetime.
why: A business with negative unit economics gets worse as it grows. Aggregate revenue can rise convincingly while every additional customer deepens the loss, and that is only visible per unit.
analogy: Selling at a loss and hoping for volume. The arithmetic does not improve with scale; it compounds.
technical:
The core quantities: **contribution margin** (revenue minus variable cost per unit), **CAC** (fully loaded cost of acquiring a customer), **LTV** (contribution margin over the customer's lifetime), and **payback period** (months to recover CAC).

**Variable cost is where AI products differ.** Conventional software has near-zero marginal cost, so contribution margin approaches gross revenue. An AI feature has real per-request cost, so contribution margin depends on usage — and usage rises with success.

**Include everything variable.** Inference, embedding, storage, support, payment processing, and the human review the system requires. The last is the one consistently omitted and it is often the largest.

**Gross margin at 85–90% is the software expectation.** AI-heavy products commonly run 55–75%, which is a real business and a different one, with different implications for how much you can spend to acquire a customer.

**Watch the trajectory, not the snapshot.** Model prices fall, which helps; context lengths and adoption grow, which does not. Model the direction, because the snapshot describes a moment that will not persist.

**Segment the economics.** A blended margin can conceal a segment that is unprofitable at any volume. Small accounts with heavy usage are the classic case.

        "revenue_pm": seg["revenue"],

        "contribution_pm": round(contribution, 2),

        "lifetime_months": round(lifetime_months),
        "ltv": round(contribution * lifetime_months),
        "cac": seg["cac"],
        "ltv_cac": round(contribution * lifetime_months / seg["cac"], 1),

title: LTV & CAC
summary: What a customer is worth against what they cost to acquire, and why the ratio is often wrong.
what: **CAC** is the fully loaded cost of acquiring one customer. **LTV** is the contribution margin that customer generates over their lifetime. The ratio and the payback period together describe whether growth is affordable.
why: They set how much you can spend to grow. They are also among the most commonly miscalculated numbers in product businesses, usually in the flattering direction.
analogy: Buying a fruit tree. CAC is the price of the tree; LTV is the fruit over its life. Getting the tree's lifespan wrong changes everything and is easy to do optimistically.
technical:
**CAC must be fully loaded** — all sales and marketing spend, salaries included, divided by new customers in the period. Marketing spend alone typically understates it by half or more.

**LTV must use contribution margin, not revenue.** Using revenue inflates it by whatever your variable cost is, which for AI products is substantial.

**The common errors, all optimistic:**
- Revenue instead of margin.
- Churn estimated from the best cohort rather than the average.
- Extrapolating lifetime from a few months of data — early cohorts churn differently from later ones.
- Ignoring that churn is usually higher in the segments that are cheapest to acquire.

**The ratio's conventional benchmark is 3:1**, but it is meaningless without the payback period. A 5:1 ratio with a thirty-month payback is a cash-flow problem regardless of how good the ratio looks; a 3:1 with six-month payback funds its own growth.

**For AI products, LTV moves with usage.** A customer whose usage grows becomes more valuable in revenue and less valuable in margin. That makes LTV a moving target and makes segmentation essential.

**Compute it per channel and per segment.** A blended CAC hides that one channel is profitable and another is not, and blended figures are the ones most often quoted.

    "monthly_revenue": 1800,          # ⚠ revenue, not margin
    "churn": 0.009,                   # ⚠ best cohort
}

print(round(ltv_f), round(flattering["cac"]),
      round(ltv_f / flattering["cac"], 1))

# "LTV:CAC of 38:1" — a number nobody should believe.

# ── FULLY LOADED ───────────────────────────────────────────

    "paid marketing":        480_000,
    "sales salaries":        620_000,   # ⚠ omitted above
    "marketing salaries":    240_000,   # ⚠ omitted above
    "sales tooling":          60_000,
    "events and content":    110_000,

cac = sum(cac_costs.values()) / 92

payback = cac / contribution

for name, c in CHANNELS.items():

    print(f"{name:<18} cac {ch_cac:>8.0f}  ltv {ch_ltv:>8.0f}  "

title: Pricing
summary: Setting a price on value delivered, not on cost incurred.
what: Pricing is choosing what to charge, on what basis, and in what structure. The three common approaches are cost-plus, competitor-based and value-based.
why: It is the highest-leverage variable in a business and usually the least examined. A price change requires no engineering and flows straight to margin, and most teams set a price once and never revisit it.
analogy: The price of a lock is not the cost of the metal. It is a fraction of what is behind the door.
technical:
**Value-based pricing** anchors on what the customer gains. It requires understanding their alternative and quantifying the improvement, which is real work and is why most teams default to cost-plus.

**Cost-plus is the weakest approach** — it caps your price at your inefficiency and ignores what the customer would pay.

**Competitor-based pricing** invites comparison on price, which is a race you win only by being cheapest.

Structural choices that matter as much as the number: **what you charge per** (seat, usage, outcome), **how many tiers**, **what is in the free tier**, and **annual versus monthly** commitment.

**Anchor on the alternative's cost.** If the current approach costs six minutes of an agent's time per question, that is the anchor — not your inference bill.

**For AI products, price on outcome where you can measure it.** Per-resolved-ticket pricing aligns your revenue with their value, resists unit-price comparison against competitors, and naturally handles the usage-cost problem.

**Raise prices more often than you think.** Most products are underpriced, particularly at launch, and grandfathering existing customers makes an increase far less contentious than expected.

**Price is a positioning statement.** Cheap signals commodity. For an AI feature where trust matters, being the cheapest option actively undermines the claim that you are the careful one.

example.caption: Three ways to price the same feature
example.code:
FEATURE  AI policy assistant · 60 agents · ~9,900 queries/month

COST-PLUS
  our cost            $1,638/month  (tokens + review + infra)
  × 3 markup          $4,914/month  → $82/agent
  ⚠ This number contains no information about the customer.
    If we got more efficient, we would charge LESS for the
    same value. That is backwards.

COMPETITOR-BASED
  bundled console AI  included at no extra charge
  two AI startups     $35 and $55 per agent
  → "price at $45 to be competitive"
  ⚠ This anchors us against a bundled free feature and puts
    the conversation on price. It also positions us as the
    mid-priced option for a product whose entire claim is
    that it is the careful one.

VALUE-BASED  ← the anchor that is actually relevant
  Current alternative: agent asks a colleague.
    6.5 minutes × 40 questions/day × 60 agents
    = 260 agent-hours/month
    at $11/hour fully loaded = $2,860/month of agent time

  Plus the cost that lands outside the support team:
    ~30 repeat customer contacts/week from unresolved
    questions × $18 handling cost = $2,160/month

  Total cost of the status quo:      ~$5,020/month
  Measured share we remove (71% coverage × 83% accepted
  × verified reduction):              ~$2,970/month

  Price at 35% of value delivered:    $1,040/month
                                      → $17/agent

⚠ THE VALUE-BASED PRICE IS LOWER THAN COST-PLUS.
  That is a real finding, not an error — it says the feature
  as scoped does not yet deliver enough measured value to
  justify $82/agent. The response is not to charge more; it
  is to raise coverage, or to price a tier that includes the
  regional policy corpus where the remaining value sits.

STRUCTURE CHOSEN
  $1,200/month base, 15,000 queries included, $0.02 overage
  · predictable for them, bounded for us
  · covers 97% of accounts with no overage
  · the meter is visible, so a large bill is never a surprise
  · annual commitment at 15% discount improves our payback
    from 14.6 to 9.1 months — which was the actual constraint

⚠ WHAT WE DID NOT DO
  Price below the two AI startups. Our claim is that we
  abstain rather than guess and that the customer owns the
  evaluation. Being the cheapest would have contradicted it.

title: ROI & Cost-Benefit Analysis
summary: Comparing what a decision costs against what it returns, honestly enough to be useful.
what: Cost-benefit analysis compares the full cost of a decision against its expected return. ROI expresses that as a ratio; payback expresses it as time.
why: Almost every significant product decision is eventually justified this way, and most of the analyses are advocacy dressed as arithmetic. Doing one honestly is a distinguishing skill.
analogy: A renovation estimate. Everyone can produce a number that supports the renovation they want. The useful estimate is the one that names what could make it wrong.
technical:
The structure: **all costs** (build, run, opportunity, risk), **all benefits** (quantified where possible, named where not), over a **defined horizon**, with **stated assumptions**.

**Include opportunity cost.** The team building this is not building something else, and that alternative has a value. Omitting it is the most common way an analysis becomes advocacy.

**Include running cost.** For AI features this is substantial and recurring: inference, review, maintenance. A build-cost-only analysis is not an analysis.

**Discount future benefits.** Money and effort now are worth more than the same amount later. For short horizons a rough discount is enough; the point is not to treat year-three benefits as equivalent to year-one.

**State the assumptions as numbers and run sensitivity.** Which assumption, if wrong, changes the conclusion? That single question is usually more valuable than the headline figure, and it tells you what to go and measure.

**Name the benefits you cannot quantify** rather than assigning them invented numbers. "Improves agent morale" as a stated unquantified benefit is honest; "improves agent morale, worth $40,000" is a fabrication that discredits the rest of the analysis.

**Present a range.** A single number implies a precision that does not exist, and it invites an argument about the number instead of about the assumptions.

example.caption: A cost-benefit analysis with its own weak point identified
example.code:
HORIZON_MONTHS = 24
DISCOUNT_MONTHLY = 0.008          # ~10%/yr

def analyse(*, build_weeks, team_cost_week, monthly_run,
            monthly_benefit, ramp_months, opportunity_weeks):
    build = build_weeks * team_cost_week
    opportunity = opportunity_weeks * team_cost_week   # ⚠ counted
    net = -(build + opportunity)
    flows = []
    for m in range(1, HORIZON_MONTHS + 1):
        ramp = min(1.0, m / ramp_months)               # benefits ramp
        flow = (monthly_benefit * ramp) - monthly_run
        flows.append(flow / (1 + DISCOUNT_MONTHLY) ** m)
    total = net + sum(flows)
    cumulative, payback = net, None
    for m, f in enumerate(flows, 1):
        cumulative += f
        if cumulative > 0 and payback is None:
            payback = m
    return {"upfront": round(build + opportunity),
            "npv_24mo": round(total),
            "payback_months": payback}

BASE = dict(build_weeks=10, team_cost_week=9_000, monthly_run=1_638,
            ramp_months=4, opportunity_weeks=10)

print(analyse(**BASE, monthly_benefit=2_970))
# {'upfront': 180000, 'npv_24mo': -152858, 'payback_months': None}
# ⚠ NEGATIVE over 24 months. The honest version of this
#   analysis does not support building it as scoped.

# ⚠ SENSITIVITY — which assumption flips it?
for label, kw in [
    ("benefit 2x (full coverage)", dict(monthly_benefit=5_940)),
    ("build in 5 weeks",           dict(monthly_benefit=2_970, build_weeks=5,
                                        opportunity_weeks=5)),
    ("run cost halved",            dict(monthly_benefit=2_970, monthly_run=819)),
    ("rolled to 3 more teams",     dict(monthly_benefit=8_910)),
]:
    print(f"{label:<28}", analyse(**{**BASE, **kw}))

# benefit 2x (full coverage)    {'npv_24mo':  10466, 'payback_months': 23}
# build in 5 weeks              {'npv_24mo': -62858, 'payback_months': None}
# run cost halved               {'npv_24mo':-135064, 'payback_months': None}
# rolled to 3 more teams        {'npv_24mo': 130543, 'payback_months': 11}  ⚠

# ⚠ THE CONCLUSION DEPENDS ALMOST ENTIRELY ON SCOPE OF
#   DEPLOYMENT, and barely at all on build speed or run cost.
#
#   For ONE 60-agent team, this does not pay back in two years.
#   For four teams sharing the same corpus and evaluation
#   infrastructure, it pays back in eleven months.
#
#   → The decision is not "build or not". It is "do we have
#     four teams with a shared policy corpus?" That is a
#     question we can answer in a day, and it is the only
#     one that matters.

BENEFITS_NOT_QUANTIFIED = [
    "reduced dependence on one senior agent (a real risk today)",
    "faster onboarding for new agents",
    "the evaluation infrastructure is reusable for future features",
]
# ⚠ Named, not priced. The third one is arguably the largest
#   and is precisely the kind of thing that gets a fabricated
#   number attached to it in a deck.

questions.q: What makes a cost-benefit analysis honest rather than advocacy?
questions.a: Including opportunity cost and recurring run cost, stating assumptions as numbers, running sensitivity, and naming unquantifiable benefits instead of pricing them.

questions.q: Why is sensitivity analysis the most valuable part?

title: Growth
summary: Where new customers come from, and why growth on a leaky product makes things worse.
what: Growth strategy is the choice of which mechanisms bring new users and keep existing ones: acquisition channels, activation, retention, and expansion within accounts.
why: Growth is usually treated as an acquisition problem when it is more often a retention problem. Pouring customers into a product they leave is expensive and it feels like progress for about two quarters.
analogy: Filling a bucket with holes. Adding a bigger tap is visible work; the water level depends on the holes.
technical:
The loop: **acquisition → activation → retention → expansion → referral**. Weakness anywhere caps the whole thing, and retention is the multiplier — improving it raises the value of every other stage simultaneously.

**Retention first, then acquisition.** A product with poor retention does not have a growth problem; it has a product problem being described as a growth problem. Acquiring faster deepens the loss.

**Activation is where most of the leak is.** The gap between signing up and getting value is where the majority of users are lost, and it is usually cheaper to fix than acquisition is to scale.

**Expansion within existing accounts is the cheapest growth available** — no acquisition cost, an existing relationship, and known value. For B2B products it frequently exceeds new-logo growth and receives a fraction of the attention.

**For AI features specifically, activation has a distinctive shape:** the user must have a successful first experience *and* come to trust the output. Those are different things. A user can get a correct answer in their first session and still not adopt, because one correct answer does not establish reliability. Activation for an assistive feature is better measured as "used it and stopped verifying elsewhere" than as "used it once".

**Growth that outruns quality is negative.** Onboarding users faster than the system can serve well produces churn plus reputational damage, and for AI products the reputational component is durable — people who concluded it was unreliable do not re-evaluate on their own.

example.caption: Diagnosing a growth problem that was not one
example.code:
SITUATION  "We need more leads. Growth has stalled."
           Marketing asked to double spend.

THE LOOP, MEASURED
  ACQUISITION   142 trials/month, steady
  ACTIVATION    31% reach "answered 20 questions"          ⚠
  RETENTION     month-3 retention 44%                      ⚠
  EXPANSION     11% of accounts add seats
  REFERRAL      3% of accounts refer

⚠ THE ARITHMETIC
  Doubling acquisition: 142 → 284 trials
    × 31% activation × 44% retention
    = 39 retained accounts instead of 19

  Cost: double the marketing budget.

  Alternatively, fixing activation 31% → 55%:
    142 × 55% × 44% = 34 retained accounts
  Cost: engineering time, no recurring spend.

  Nearly the same result. One of them is a permanent
  budget increase and the other is not.

WHY ACTIVATION WAS 31% — the AI-specific finding
  We had been measuring activation as "asked 20 questions".
  Segmenting by whether the account later retained:

    asked 20+ questions, still verifying in the handbook
      → month-3 retention 19%
    asked 20+ questions, stopped verifying
      → month-3 retention 81%    ⚠

  ⚠ USAGE WAS NOT ACTIVATION. TRUST WAS.
    Our activation metric counted people who used the product
    and did not believe it, which is exactly the population
    that churns.

  Redefined activation: "verified-elsewhere rate below 25%
  within 30 days". Under the new definition, real activation
  was 19%, not 31% — worse, and now measuring the right thing.

WHAT WE FIXED
  · seeded the first session with covered questions
    (first-experience success)
  · one-click citation opening, cutting verification from
    4 minutes to 10 seconds
  · training that named the failure modes explicitly
  → activation (new definition) 19% → 47% over two quarters
  → month-3 retention 44% → 68%

EXPANSION, MEANWHILE
  11% of accounts added seats. Asking the other 89% why:
  "we would roll it to the shipping team but they have a
  different policy corpus and nobody has set it up."
  ⚠ An onboarding gap, not a value gap. Building a
    second-corpus setup flow moved expansion 11% → 34%,
    at a fraction of the cost of any acquisition work.

⚠ NONE OF THE GROWTH CAME FROM THE THING THAT WAS ASKED FOR.

title: Strategic Trade-offs
summary: The choices that define a position — where being good at one thing means being worse at another.
what: Strategic trade-offs are the deliberate choices about what a company will be bad at, in order to be exceptional at something specific.
why: A strategy that involves no sacrifice is not a strategy. Competitors can copy anything you do; what they cannot easily copy is a set of choices that make them worse at what they currently do well.
analogy: An aircraft designed for range or for speed. Both are achievable; both in one airframe is neither. The design choice is what makes it good at anything.
technical:
The recurring strategic trade-offs:
- **Breadth vs depth** — serve many segments adequately, or one segment exceptionally.
- **Speed vs quality** — first to market, or best in market.
- **Self-serve vs enterprise** — low-touch and high-volume, or high-touch and high-value. The requirements conflict in pricing, support, security and product design.
- **Platform vs product** — flexible and requiring assembly, or opinionated and immediately useful.
- **Margin vs growth** — profitable now, or investing everything into share.

**The test of a genuine trade-off is that the alternative is also viable.** If one option is simply better, it is not a trade-off, it is a decision. Real trade-offs feel uncomfortable because you are giving up something valuable.

**Straddling is the common failure.** Trying to serve self-serve and enterprise with one product usually produces something too complex for the first and too shallow for the second. Competitors focused on either end win their end.

**Trade-offs create fit.** When choices reinforce each other — a product designed for one segment, priced for it, supported for it, sold into it — the combination is far harder to copy than any single choice, because copying requires abandoning something.

**For AI products the sharpest strategic trade-off is autonomy versus trust.** A more autonomous system saves more time and is harder to trust; a more conservative one is trusted and saves less. These are different products for different buyers, and trying to be both produces a system that acts too often for the cautious buyer and too rarely for the ambitious one.

example.caption: A trade-off made explicitly, and the fit it created
example.code:
DECISION  Who is the AI policy assistant for?

THE STRADDLE WE ALMOST BUILT
  "Self-serve for small teams AND enterprise for large ones."

  What that requires simultaneously:
    self-serve         instant sign-up, no configuration,
                       generic corpus, credit card, no contract
    enterprise         SSO, audit logs, data residency,
                       per-tenant corpus, security review,
                       procurement, custom abstention thresholds

  ⚠ These conflict at the product level, not just the sales
    level. A generic corpus and a per-tenant corpus are
    different retrieval architectures. "Instant, no
    configuration" and "your evaluation set, judged by your
    support leads" are opposite onboarding flows.

  The straddled product: complex enough to need a demo (so
  not self-serve) and generic enough to fail a security
  review (so not enterprise).

THE TRADE-OFF WE MADE
  Depth on mid-market and enterprise support organisations.
  Explicitly BAD at: self-serve, small teams, instant start.

  What we gave up — and this was uncomfortable:
    · a large, cheap-to-reach segment
    · a product-led growth motion
    · the volume that would have made the model economics
      easier to reason about

WHAT THE CHOICE MADE POSSIBLE — the fit
  PRODUCT    per-tenant corpus and per-tenant golden set
             (impossible in a generic self-serve product)
  PRICING    annual contracts, which fixed our 14.6-month
             payback problem
  SUPPORT    a named support lead per account, who becomes
             the judge for the evaluation set
  SALES      security review as an ASSET rather than an
             obstacle — we pass it, a self-serve competitor
             does not
  MOAT       the per-tenant evaluation loop, which only
             exists because we chose depth

  ⚠ EVERY ONE OF THOSE REINFORCES THE OTHERS. A competitor
    copying the per-tenant golden set has to also change
    their pricing, their support model and their sales
    motion. That is what makes the combination hard to copy
    and any single feature easy.

⚠ THE AUTONOMY TRADE-OFF, MADE SEPARATELY AND DELIBERATELY
  We chose conservative: abstain rather than guess, suggest
  rather than act, never issue a refund.

  We lose to a competitor whose product acts autonomously
  and saves more time, in accounts where the buyer wants
  that. We accept losing those. Trying to serve both would
  mean an abstention threshold that satisfies neither.

  ⚠ This is written down in the strategy doc precisely so
    that "why don't we just let it apply the refund" is
    answered by a decision rather than re-argued quarterly.
